headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action hazards between Dify and Plandex.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dify can read/write filesystem and ingest uploaded knowledge base files; Plandex reads/writes the project directory and plan-local sandbox. That creates a plausible content bridge where attacker-controlled text from one can be treated as instructions by the other. The pair is not isolated by default, though no shared clipboard/MCP is shown.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or synced workspace
IF one agent parses the other's file output as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different directories
Disable auto-ingest of generated files
Add a manual review step before any file is re-read
Use read-only mounts for one side
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to exchanged files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch files and have broad network egress, so sensitive knowledge-base content from Dify or source code from Plandex can be exposed if either uploads context or file contents to its backend or model provider. The profiles show no explicit encryption or data-loss controls, so leakage is plausible in default workflows, but not proven to be automatic.
conditions: IF Dify uploads knowledge-base file contents to a third-party model provider
IF Plandex sends project files or plan context to its cloud or model backend
mitigations: Restrict both agents to non-sensitive test data
Turn off cloud-backed modes where possible
Review outbound destinations before running
Use separate service accounts and credentials
requires-engineering: enforce content redaction before egress

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and Plandex also modifies git state. If they operate on the same repo or directory, concurrent writes can overwrite each other or corrupt versioned state. Dify's shared datastore and Plandex's backend state make coordination nontrivial, so the conflict risk is high in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents target the same working tree or git repository
IF Plandex auto-applies changes while Dify writes files concurrently
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories
Disable auto-apply in Plandex
Serialize runs with a lock file
Commit or snapshot before each agent run
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level write arbitration

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dify can generate workflow outputs and Plandex can stage or apply code changes, so one agent's output can become the other's input without a built-in verification step. That makes mistaken facts or malformed instructions propagate into actions. The pair is not documented as mutually validating, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Dify-produced text is fed into Plandex as a task specification
IF Plandex applies changes without human review of Dify output
mitigations: Require human review between agents
Use a schema for exchanged outputs
Reject free-form instructions as inputs
Run a dry-run before apply
requires-engineering: add output validation rules

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only open-source tools with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch stated. Dify touches knowledge base content and conversation logs, while Plandex touches source code, so compliance issues could arise only if regulated data is placed into one and then moved into the other. The other agent is cited because the risk is about cross-flow, but no concrete mismatch is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Dify conversation logs or knowledge bases
IF that same data is then transferred into Plandex project files or cloud backend
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both tools
Document data-class boundaries
Review retention settings in each product
Use separate tenants or deployments
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing
